source.title: Economics – Core Concepts
allPromptTexts: List and define 30 key terms in economics.
List and provide clear explanations of 15 key concepts in economics.
Provide the top ten mathematical equations essential to economics.
Provide a salient description of the world of economics today.
How does the skillset of the typical economist differ today from 50 years ago?
Create a 10-item quiz on the discussion above.
Provide 15 discussion questions relevant to the content above.
source.preamble: Original highlight extracts read; replaced with clearly labeled edited highlights. Original contents replaced with exact prompt navigation.

responseDecisions.1.1: Retained all thirty original terms/order; corrected opportunity cost, trade-balance sign, diminishing returns, unemployment, supply/demand, monetary policy, economic systems and liquidity. Retained accurate basic definitions.
responseDecisions.1.2: Retained thirty terms/order; clarified rational choice, demand versus quantity, proportional elasticity, public goods, statistical unemployment, irregular cycles and alternative forms of socialism.
responseDecisions.2.1: Preserved fifteen concepts; developed town-building, evening-time, elasticity and comparative-advantage examples; distinguished GDP/welfare, marginal/total output, equilibrium/stability and public ownership/public-good properties.
responseDecisions.2.2: Preserved fifteen concepts; corrected luxury-good exception, scarce-resource claim and price response; retained effective supply-time-horizon, externality, monopoly and micro/macro explanations.
responseDecisions.3.1: Retained ten equations in order. Defined inverse demand; corrected GDP components, surplus triangles, finite/local marginal cost, NPV bounds and multiplier assumptions. Clarified simple versus compound interest and constant returns. Repaired repeated list numbering.
responseDecisions.3.2: Retained ten equations and grouped structure. Distinguished utility ranking from measured happiness, MC=MR condition from sufficient optimum, planned AD from GDP identity, and short/long-run supply assumptions.
responseDecisions.4.1: Preserved seven-paragraph progression from academia through industry/public policy to interdisciplinary and methodological issues. Replaced promotional claims with concrete estimation tasks, dated 2024 scope and uncertainty.
responseDecisions.4.2: Kept all academia/industry/challenges lists. Removed unprecedented-accuracy and profit/stability promises; added dated research examples, credible comparisons and distinction between firm interests and public effects.
responseDecisions.5.1: Kept six historical comparison pairs and summary. Anchored 1974–2024; corrected manual/analog, no-empirical-past and newly-invented-fields caricatures. Skills vary by role and do not guarantee inference.
responseDecisions.5.2: Preserved Focus/Toolset/Skillset progression. Corrected past-versus-future and theory-versus-data dichotomies; documented reproducibility policy, data bias and role-specific skills.
responseDecisions.6.1: Preserved ten questions, option counts and ten keys. Broadened narrow skills-only quiz to cover the full thread; checked every answer, fixed unsupported universality and numbered fragmented lists consecutively.
responseDecisions.6.2: Preserved ten multiple-choice questions; corrected no-valid-answer items 1 and 7, big-data guarantee and ambiguous industry example. Added explicitly labeled missing ten-answer key after source quiz.
responseDecisions.7.1: Fifteen questions retained in order; three adjusted to remove universal skill and automatic accuracy premises. Twelve verbatim.
responseDecisions.7.2: Fifteen questions retained in order; two adjusted to invite trade-offs and conditional trade effects. Thirteen verbatim.

addedAnswerKey: Gemini supplied ten quiz questions without answers. Ten answers appended, explicitly labeled editorial addition; all original lists remain intact.
remainingConcerns: Historical comparison explicitly anchors today to March 2024 and fifty years earlier to roughly 1974. It is not a current economic forecast or a survey of every economist.
GDP, unemployment and institutional examples specify applicable definitions; policy implications depend on assumptions.
Deposit multiplier retained as a restrictive textbook exercise, not a mechanical description of modern banking.
